bracket: [Textbook note — the printed answer is \(5\,\text{m}\), and the UNIT is wrong on any reading of the question. The question asks for a molarity, and \(5\) is a molarity (\(\text{mol L}^{-1}\)), not a molality: the molality here is \(4.00\,\text{m}\) if "per kg of water" means per kg of solvent, and \(4.41\,\text{m}\) if it means per kg of lake water, and neither is \(5\). The VALUE is right, and reaching it settles the stem's genuine ambiguity: only the second reading — "water" = the lake water, i.e. the solution — gives \(V = 1000/1.25 = 800\,\text{mL}\) and \(M = 4.0/0.800 = 5.00\) exactly. The solution below therefore takes that reading and names the other one, which returns \(4.58\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).]

[Textbook note — the data in this question are not physically consistent, though the answer is unaffected. A \(5\%\) (by mass) cane-sugar solution is \(5/342.3\) mol in \(0.095\,\text{kg}\) of water, i.e. \(0.1538\,\text{m}\); a freezing point of \(271\,\text{K}\) is a depression of \(2.15\,\text{K}\) and so implies \(K_f = 13.98\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\) for water, against its real value of \(1.86\). With the true \(K_f\) that solution would freeze at \(272.86\,\text{K}\), not \(271\,\text{K}\). The question is posed and answered as a RATIO of the two depressions, in which \(K_f\) cancels, so the printed answer of \(269.07\,\text{K}\) stands and matches the derivation below — but a student checking the given freezing point against a table of \(K_f\) values will find it does not reconcile, and that is the book's inconsistency rather than an error in the answer.]
